We also identify a notable discrepancy between the optimized strategy and the one yielding the highest payoff in the population, highlighting the importance of distributing tasks based on their difficulty levels. Our research provides actionable advice on task allocation and the use of customized distribution models. We propose several future directions for research and offer a user guide for implementing the proposed methods.

Neural language models have been incredibly successful in classification tasks, especially multi-task learning, but face limitations when applied to low-resource languages. One proposed solution is to use a high-resource language model and fine-tune it on available data from the target language. However, when working with sentiment classification and the model is not native to the language being studied, this approach doesn't function effectively. To address this challenge, we introduce a new technique called "Induced Multitask Learning" that enables a model to classify sentiments in a language it has not been trained on. This method involves training the model on a similar language where sentiment data is abundant, and then adapting it to the target language. We conduct experiments with a neural language model on Portuguese and find that it performs significantly better in sentiment classification when pre-trained on French compared to monolingual training. The results show that inducing multitask learning on French significantly improves the model's accuracy in classification tasks. The code and data are available for review.

Recent advances in AI research have led to the development of various models that can effectively process question-answering tasks, some of which even leverage pre-trained models on large text datasets. Notably, some studies have employed pre-trained models on knowledge graphs represented as factual triples, which have shown promising results in question-answering tasks, especially for categories like definition, description, and simple questions. However, given the limited information available in knowledge graphs, these models may struggle with more complex question types such as count, compare, and abstract questions. In contrast to models pre-trained on knowledge graphs, those trained on traditional text data have been found to yield better performance for more demanding question types. This research aims to bridge the knowledge gap between these two models by investigating the capabilities of models pre-trained on knowledge graphs in comparison to those pre-trained on general text data for various question-answering tasks. Notably, we conduct experiments using both single-models and multi-models, and evaluate the performance of these models on a wide range of question types including definition, description, simple, count, compare, and abstract questions. The results reveal that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs outperform models pre-trained on general text data for majority of the question types, except for the abstract question type. Furthermore, we find that the single-model (T5) delivers superior performance compared to the multi-model (BERT) for almost all question types, except for the description question type. Lastly, we observe that the models pre-trained on knowledge graphs with the highest performance achieve better results when incorporating external knowledge in the form of text snippets in comparison to using automatic generation of question answers. This research contributes to the development of efficient question-answering systems that can processing various question types and provides actionable advice for constructing and utilizing knowledge graphs. Moreover, we curate a large-scale dataset consisting of 100,000 questions and answers, along with their corresponding knowledge graphs, which is available for public use.

This paper presents new branching fraction measurements for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^-* \gamma$ decays, which involve the $D_s^*$ resonance, as well as the measurement of the branching fraction ratio between the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^- \rho^0$ and $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^- \gamma$ decays. The data used for this study consists of $pp$ collisions collected by the LHCb detector at a center-of-mass energy of 7 and 8 TeV. The decays of interest were identified based on candidates that included the $D_s^-}$, $D_s(^{*})\rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-$, and $\rho^0\rightarrow \pi^+ \pi^-$ decays. The calculation of branching fraction ratios involved the use of the known $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^- \gamma$ branching fraction, which is subject to uncertainties associated with the $D_s$ and $\gamma$ branching fractions.
